blogPosts.title: The environment variable that was set, and wasn’t
blogPosts.excerpt: A Spring Boot service came up healthy in production with its CORS origins still pointing at localhost, its WebAuthn relying party still localhost, and its rate limiter switched off — with every one of those variables present in the environment.

blogPosts.title: Six requests and a limit of five
blogPosts.excerpt: A rate limiter set to five requests per day sounded generous for a demo nobody would use twice. It meant no visitor could finish the demo even once — and it was trivially bypassable at the same time.
blogPosts.content:
I put a fixed-window rate limiter in front of a public authentication demo. Five requests per IP per day. It seemed conservative-but-fine: the demo is a walkthrough, nobody runs it twice.

Then a visitor reported being blocked partway through. So did I, from my phone, on a different network, as a different user.

## Two bugs wearing the same coat

**The first was arithmetic.** The limiter counts *requests*. A complete run of the demo is:

```
POST /auth/register
POST /auth/login
POST /passkey/register/init
POST /passkey/register/complete
POST /passkey/login/init
POST /passkey/login/complete
```

Six. The limit was five. The last request of the passkey login — the one that proves the whole thing works — was the one refused. The demo was not rate limited; it was **impossible**, and had been since the day the limiter was switched on.

The number was not too small. It was **measured in the wrong unit**. I now express it in the unit the operator actually thinks in:

```
# MAX_REQUESTS counts REQUESTS, not visitors. One full run of the demo costs
# SIX of them, so set it in units of runs:
#
#     30 requests / 6 per run  =  5 complete demo runs per IP per 24h
AUTH_PLATFORM_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS=30
```

A value below six is not a strict setting. It is a trap: it lets nobody finish, while looking like a policy decision.

**The second bug was the key.** Two different people, on two different networks, shared a bucket. The limiter was keying on this:

```java
String forwarded = request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
```

Behind a reverse proxy, `X-Forwarded-For` is a **list that the proxy appends to**. Its left-most entry is whatever the caller sent. So the header is partly caller-controlled: vary it per request and every attempt lands in a fresh bucket, which makes the limiter decorative. And when nobody sends one, everyone collapses into a single shared key, which is what my visitor and I hit.

Worse, the framework had already eaten it. Spring's `ForwardedHeaderFilter` — which you want, because it is what stops same-origin requests looking cross-origin behind a proxy — **consumes and removes** the `X-Forwarded-*` headers. By the time the rate-limit filter ran, there was nothing to read.

## Getting the key from something the caller cannot set

The proxy knows the real peer address. It just has to state it in a header it **overwrites** rather than appends to:

```
reverse_proxy auth-service:8080 {
	# The rate limiter keys on this. X-Forwarded-For cannot be used: Caddy
	# APPENDS to it, so its left-most entry is whatever the caller sent, and
	# ForwardedHeaderFilter strips the X-Forwarded-* headers before the limiter
	# runs anyway. header_up OVERWRITES, and {remote_host} is the real TCP peer.
	header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
}
```

and the filter prefers it:

```java
String realIp = request.getHeader("X-Real-IP");
if (realIp != null && !realIp.isBlank()) {
    return realIp.trim();
}
```

`{remote_host}` is the TCP peer as the proxy sees it. A client cannot forge it, because it is not something the client sends.

## What I took from it

Neither bug was visible in development. Locally there is no proxy, so the header behaves; and I never ran the demo end to end against a limiter that was actually switched on — in development it defaulted to off.

Two habits came out of this. **Express a limit in the unit of the thing being limited**: five visitors is a policy, five requests is an implementation detail, and confusing them silently broke the feature. And **never derive a security decision from a header the caller can write** — either take it from the transport, or have infrastructure you trust overwrite it before it reaches you.

blogPosts.title: Why the browser carries a code, not a token
blogPosts.excerpt: Wiring my own site into my own auth service, the shortest path was to hand the browser a JWT and be done. Here is what a redirect URL actually does with whatever you put in it, and what the code exchange buys instead.
blogPosts.content:
I had an authentication service with working passkeys, and a separate site whose admin panel needed a login. Both mine, both on the same box. The obvious shortcut: authenticate on the auth service, redirect back with the token in the query string, done in an afternoon.

I built the longer version instead, and the reason is worth writing down.

## A redirect URL is not a private channel

When you send a browser to `https://example.com/callback?token=eyJhbGciOi...`, that string does not travel from A to B and disappear. It is written to **browser history**. It is sent as the `Referer` header on the next outbound request from that page. It is recorded in the **access log of every proxy** on the path, and in the destination server's own logs, which are usually the least-protected copy of anything you own.

An access token in that position is a live credential sitting in four places you were not thinking about. The fix is not to protect the URL. It is to put something in it that is **not worth stealing**.

## What a code is

The redirect carries a one-time authorisation code with three properties:

- it can be redeemed **exactly once**
- it expires in about **a minute**
- it is worthless without a **client secret** that never leaves the relying party's server

So the flow gains a step. The browser comes back with a code; the relying party's *backend* exchanges it for tokens, server to server, authenticating with its secret. Nothing sensitive was ever in the URL, and a code copied out of a proxy log is an expired, spent, useless string.

```
1. /admin, no session      -> redirect to the auth service
2. passkey login           -> one-time code, in the redirect back
3. server-side exchange    -> code + client secret -> tokens
```

## The three checks that carry the weight

**Exact redirect URI matching.** The most exploited bug in this shape of flow is an open redirect: get the authorisation server to send the code somewhere the operator never registered. A prefix comparison feels safe and is not — `https://example.com/` is a prefix of `https://example.com/@attacker.test`, which browsers resolve to a completely different host. A host comparison ignores the path. Full string equality, or nothing:

```java
if (redirectUri == null || !properties.getRedirectUris().contains(redirectUri)) {
    throw new CustomException(400, "redirect_uri is not registered for this client");
}
```

**Single use, enforced by the database.** "Single use" is a claim about concurrency, so a boolean check does not establish it. Redemption is read-then-write: select where `consumed = false`, then update by primary key. Under PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED, two requests presenting the same code can both read it as unconsumed and both mint a session. The row lock is what makes that impossible:

```java
@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
Optional<SsoAuthCodeEntity> findByCodeHashAndConsumedFalse(String codeHash);
```

The second request blocks; when the first commits, Postgres re-evaluates the predicate against the new row version, so the loser sees no row and gets the same rejection as an unknown code. And the table stores a **SHA-256 of the code**, never the code — a database dump should not come with usable credentials attached.

**`state`, and it is not optional.** The relying party generates a random value, stores it in an httpOnly cookie, sends it along, and refuses the callback unless what comes back matches. Without it, an attacker starts their own login and hands the victim the resulting callback URL — the victim ends up signed into the **attacker's** account, and everything they then write goes there. I made it a required parameter rather than a recommended one, because an optional security parameter is one that eventually gets left out.

## The check that made the whole thing worth building

My auth service has open registration — it is a public demo. So a signature-valid token proves exactly one thing: **somebody signed up**. That is not a reason to let them into a CMS.

What the relying party actually needs is a claim about authorisation, so the token carries one:

```java
.claim("roles", List.copyOf(roles))
```

and the client declares what it requires. The claim is always present, even when empty, so a consumer reads one shape instead of treating "no roles" as a different case from "no claim" — and the branch that handles a missing claim is invariably the one that defaults to letting someone in.

## Was it worth it over an afternoon's shortcut

The short version would have worked, in the sense that I could have logged in. It would also have written a live credential into my own access logs, offered no way to revoke a session, and made "who is allowed in" a property of who happened to know the URL.

The long version is perhaps three hundred lines and it is now the thing I would point at in an interview.

blogPosts.title: Bridging a live SSE feed into Kafka
blogPosts.excerpt: Wikipedia publishes every edit as a public Server-Sent Events stream. Turning that into a Kafka topic takes about forty lines — and the interesting part is everything those forty lines quietly decide on your behalf.
blogPosts.content:
Wikimedia publishes a live feed of every edit across all its wikis as a public Server-Sent Events stream. It is a genuinely useful thing to point a pipeline at: real volume, real bursts, no credentials, and it never stops.

I built a small producer that consumes that stream and republishes each event onto a Kafka topic. The bridge itself is short.

## The shape

```
Wikimedia EventStreams (SSE)  -->  handler  -->  Kafka topic
     persistent HTTP              OkHttp/SSE      producer API
```

An SSE client holds one long-lived HTTP connection; the server pushes events down it. Each event arrives in a callback, and the callback hands it to a Kafka producer:

```java
@Override
public void onMessage(String event, MessageEvent messageEvent) {
    producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, messageEvent.getData()));
}
```

That is the whole bridge. What makes it worth studying is that this line makes four decisions without appearing to.

## What `send` with no callback decides

`producer.send()` is asynchronous. It writes the record into an in-memory accumulator and returns immediately; a background thread batches records and ships them. Discarding the returned `Future` and passing no callback means **delivery failures are invisible**. A broker rejecting the record, a serialization error, retries exhausted — all of it lands in a future nobody reads.

For a demo pipeline that is a fine trade. For anything that matters it is the first thing to change:

```java
producer.send(record, (metadata, exception) -> {
    if (exception != null) {
        LOGGER.error("delivery failed for topic {}", topic, exception);
    }
});
```

The asymmetry is worth internalising: **the producer will tell you about failures, but only if you ask.**

## What a null key decides

`new ProducerRecord<>(topic, value)` has no key. Kafka's partitioner therefore spreads records across partitions on its own, and Kafka only guarantees ordering **within a partition**.

For a feed of independent edits that is exactly right — it maximises parallelism and nothing depends on order. The moment you want all edits to a given page, or from a given user, to arrive in order at one consumer, you need that value as the key:

```java
new ProducerRecord<>(topic, wiki, messageEvent.getData());
```

The choice of key is really a choice about **what your consumers are allowed to assume**, made at write time and difficult to change afterwards.

## What the lifecycle decides

The producer is closed in the SSE client's `onClosed` callback. `close()` flushes what is still buffered, so an orderly shutdown loses nothing. A `kill -9`, or a JVM that exits without the stream closing cleanly, drops whatever was still in the accumulator — a window of milliseconds, but a real one. A shutdown hook is the usual answer, and if you cannot afford that window at all, then you have decided you need `acks=all` and synchronous confirmation, which is a different pipeline with different throughput.

## Why I would still start here

There is a version of this with retries, idempotent producers, a schema registry, a dead-letter topic and exactly-once semantics. It is also a version where you cannot see what any single moving part does.

Forty lines that visibly make four wrong-for-production decisions taught me more about Kafka's defaults than a correct configuration would have, precisely because each one had to be found by asking "what happens if this fails?" and following the answer. That is the value of building the small version first: the production version is mostly a list of answers to questions the small version forces you to ask.

The pipeline and a companion module of producer/consumer patterns — partitioning, callbacks, graceful shutdown, cooperative rebalancing — are on [GitHub](https://github.com/kaushal-bhatt/kafka-wikimedia-stream-pipeline).

content.heading: About
content.subtitle: Passionate about building scalable, high-performance applications that solve real-world problems
content.journey:
I’m a Senior Backend Engineer with 7 years designing and operating event-driven microservices where correctness is non-negotiable — crypto custody, KYC/AML pipelines, payment flows, and fraud detection processing millions of transactions a day.

My work sits at the intersection of distributed systems and security: Kafka/MSK event backbones, service-to-service authentication, secrets management, and the unglamorous cryptographic plumbing that keeps accounts safe. Throughout my career I’ve worked with RockWallet, EPAM Systems, Ibosstech Solutions, Boutiqaat and Lenskart, consistently delivering high-performance solutions that drive business growth.

At RockWallet I own services inside a 17-microservice monorepo and wrote the platform-wide JWT + WebAuthn authentication framework — the same expertise behind my open-source [auth-platform](https://github.com/kaushal-bhatt/auth-platform) project, which you can [try with a real passkey](https://auth.wekt.in). Open to Senior Backend Engineer roles across the EU — Blue Card eligible, English B2, German A1–A2 (in progress).
